scenes.title: Day 1 · London · Wednesday 2 October 1872
scenes.learning_goal: Know the date, the deadline and the stake in one breath; feel a clock already running.

narration.script: It is Wednesday, the second of October, 1872. Twenty-nine minutes past eleven in the morning. On a quiet street in Mayfair a French valet is being hired by a man who runs his life by the clock, and the valet's watch is four minutes slow. Keep that watch in mind. By a quarter to nine tonight, that same man will have staked half his fortune that the whole world fits into eighty days. Eighty days. Nineteen hundred and twenty hours. A hundred and fifteen thousand two hundred minutes. Look at the map: only London is lit. Over the next eighty days we will light the rest, one port at a time. Jules Verne printed this journey in a Paris newspaper that same winter, as if it were happening. The novel is our guidebook; we travel today. First, Savile Row.

scenes.title: Savile Row — the address Verne got wrong
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Verne put Fogg at No. 7 and Sheridan's death there in 1814, that Sheridan lived at No. 14 and died in 1816, and that the Row was already tailoring country; feel the hush of cloth and chalk.

narration.script: Here we are: the corner of Burlington Gardens and Savile Row. Verne opens the novel on this spot — 'No. 7, Saville Row, Burlington Gardens, the house in which Sheridan died in 1814.' He spells the street with two Ls, and he is wrong twice more. Sheridan the playwright lived at No. 14, not No. 7, and he died there in 1816, not 1814. Watch the doors as we walk and look for the numbers: No. 14 carries the plaque, put up in 1881. There is no plaque for Fogg anywhere. So the novel is our guidebook, not our gospel; we will correct it with a smile whenever we can. Look in the windows now — bolts of cloth, chalk marks, half-made jackets. This was already tailoring country in 1872. Henry Poole put his front door on the Row in 1846 and is still here — since 1982 at No. 15. Poole's own story is that in 1865 they cut the Prince of Wales a short evening jacket — the ancestor, they say, of the dinner jacket. One small detour in time: on the roof of No. 3, on the thirtieth of January 1969, the Beatles played their rooftop concert. Fogg's house, in the book, ran on the newest kit of its day — gas for light and warmth, electric bells, speaking-tubes — and held not a single book, because his club had two libraries. Here is the Row around 1890, a few years after Fogg. Same doors. Same hush.

scenes.title: Fogg's day, by the clock — enter Passepartout
scenes.learning_goal: Know Fogg's timetable and who Passepartout is; feel precision as comedy and like the valet at once.

narration.script: Fogg's day, by the clock. Tap any line to see what happens. He rises at eight. Tea and toast at twenty-three minutes past. Shaving-water at nine thirty-seven, at thirty degrees — eighty-six Fahrenheit. Out of the door at half past eleven, home at midnight. Into this house, at twenty-nine minutes past eleven, walks Passepartout: a Parisian of Paris, about thirty. Once a wandering singer, then a circus-rider who vaulted like Léotard, a rope-dancer like Blondin. Then a fireman in Paris, then ten English households in five years. He wants a quiet life. Look at his face on the card; we like him already — the man with the slow watch.

scenes.title: Count the steps — Savile Row to the Reform
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Fogg's 1,151 steps are close to the real kilometre and that Pall Mall is clubland lit by gas since 1807; feel the pace of a man who never hurries.

narration.script: Fogg leaves at half past eleven and counts his steps: five hundred and seventy-five with the right foot, five hundred and seventy-six with the left. One thousand one hundred and fifty-one. We will count them with him; watch the counter in the corner. Look up the Row first, then turn to face numbers seven and eight. Today No. 7 is not the house Verne imagined — look for yourself. Now walk south. Sixty-seven steps, and here is Verne's corner: Savile Row, Burlington Gardens. Fogg turns right. Two hundred and eight. Old Bond Street — turn left, and downhill towards Piccadilly. Four hundred and five. Piccadilly. Cross over, step a few paces west, and turn down St James's Street. St James's Street, the long straight slope. Six hundred and twenty-nine, and Fogg has not hurried once. Keep going. Seven hundred and eighty-nine. This is Pall Mall, one of the first streets in London lit by gas, back in 1807. Sixty-five years before Fogg, the lamps here were already the future. Turn east; the clubs are on your right and the counter is climbing. Pall Mall is clubland: the Reform, the Travellers and the Athenaeum stand in a row, and one turn of the head covers all three. Stop. Face the Portland-stone palazzo with the tall windows: the Reform Club, 104 Pall Mall, by Charles Barry, opened in 1841. Turn a little left: 106, the Travellers, Barry's first palazzo, 1832. Beyond it, 107, the Athenaeum. And the counter reads one thousand one hundred and fifty-one. Fogg made it 1,151. We make it about a kilometre — eleven hundred metres between the corners. Close enough for a man who never hurries.

scenes.title: Inside the Reform — what Verne got right
scenes.learning_goal: Know the Reform Club is real, founded 1836, Barry's palazzo of 1841, Soyer's kitchens, and Fogg's breakfast; feel cosy club warmth.

narration.script: We arrive at the door. The Reform Club is real, and still here: 104 Pall Mall, founded in 1836 by the men who had backed the Reform Act of 1832 — neutral today, and that is our one line of politics. Charles Barry's palazzo opened in 1841: Portland stone outside; inside, a saloon two storeys high, ringed by columns under a glass roof, and the famous kitchens that Alexis Soyer helped to plan. Look up — the tall windows of the first floor. Now Fogg's breakfast, taken here at the club: a broiled fish with Reading sauce — keep that in mind — roast beef, a tart, Cheshire cheese, and the tea the Reform is famous for. Reading sauce was a real thing, from Berkshire. Then he cuts the pages himself and reads The Times. Here is the front today; here is Barry's elevation; and here, kept small, is the saloon as engraved in 1841. We have no footage of the inside, so the engraving carries the saloon.

scenes.title: Quiz — which of Verne's club details is real?
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Verne's Reform is half fantasy (porphyry columns, blue glass) and half exact (nine garden windows); know you can visit during Open House.

narration.script: Verne describes the club in loving detail: mosaic floors, a gallery under a dome held up by twenty red porphyry columns, blue painted windows, a dining-room with nine windows onto a garden already gilded with autumn. Compare that with Barry's real building. Which of these details is real? Take your time; the tea is famous.
narration.after_script: Half fantasy, half exact — treat the novel that way for the next seventy-nine days. And one practical note: you can stand in that saloon yourself, one weekend a year, when the club opens for guided tours during Open House London; the caption has this year's dates. The tour, they say, includes one very long staircase.

scenes.title: The wager — twenty thousand at Baring's
scenes.learning_goal: Know the fictional trigger, the six names, £20,000 at Baring's, and the deadline; feel the click of a plan.

narration.script: Evening, at the whist table. In the novel — and only in the novel — a gentleman has walked out of the Bank of England three days ago with fifty-five thousand pounds, and the Daily Telegraph has printed a timetable showing the world can be circled in eighty days. Andrew Stuart, an engineer, wagers four thousand pounds that it cannot be done. Fogg raises him: twenty thousand pounds, on deposit at Baring's — half his fortune — in 'eighty days or less; in nineteen hundred and twenty hours, or a hundred and fifteen thousand two hundred minutes'. Look at the card: six names on the memorandum — Stuart first, Fogg last. Due back 'in this very room of the Reform Club, on Saturday, the 21st of December, at a quarter before nine p.m.' Verne's arithmetic holds: it is exactly eighty days, and it really was a Saturday. Fogg's motto for the evening: 'The unforeseen does not exist.' One footnote from today. Baring's, Fogg's bank, was one of London's oldest; it went under in 1995. The wager has outlived the bank.

scenes.title: The world had just shrunk — the 80-day loop
scenes.learning_goal: Know the three enablers of 1869–70 and the eight legs that add up to eighty; feel the thrill of the map lighting up.

narration.script: How could anyone even think it? Because the world had just shrunk. When a partner said the world was big, Fogg's answer was three words: 'It was once.' Look at the three lights. The Suez Canal, opened in November 1869. The American railroad, joined at Promontory Summit in May 1869. The last rail link across India, closed at Jabalpur in March 1870. Three doors, opened within ten months, two years before tonight. Now watch the line draw. London to Suez, by rail and steamer through Mont Cenis and Brindisi, seven days. Suez to Bombay by steamer, thirteen. Bombay to Calcutta by rail, three. Calcutta to Hong Kong, thirteen. Hong Kong to Yokohama, six. Yokohama to San Francisco, twenty-two. San Francisco to New York by rail, seven. New York back to London, nine. Add them up: eighty. Now tap the longest leg on the map.
narration.after_script: The Pacific — twenty-two days of ocean; keep this in mind for later. And the map fades back to tonight: only London lit. Because Fogg, still at the table, says the sentence that turns the evening. 'The train leaves for Dover at a quarter before nine.'

scenes.title: Ten minutes — pack the carpet-bag
scenes.learning_goal: Know what went into the carpet-bag and what stayed at Savile Row; feel the scramble.

narration.script: Twenty-five past seven. Fogg goes home from the club, calls Passepartout and says: 'We start for Dover and Calais in ten minutes.' Where to? 'We are going round the world.' 'In eighty days.' Passepartout, remember, wanted a quiet life. Now help him pack. One carpet-bag, and it must hold everything. Drag in what goes; leave what stays. Verne gives the list; ours keeps the six things that matter. Two shirts and three pairs of stockings each, a mackintosh, a travelling-cloak, the red-bound Bradshaw's Continental Guide — the world's timetable, hundreds of pages of trains and hotels — and a goodly roll of Bank of England notes: twenty thousand pounds. No books, because there are none in the house. The electric clock stays on the mantel. And so, tonight, does the gas — remember that. Two shirts, three pairs of stockings, and half a fortune.

scenes.title: Charing Cross — Fogg's newest London
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Fogg's London was brand-new (station 8, Underground 9, Embankment 2, Big Ben 13) and remember the twenty guineas; feel awe at a new city and one warm beat.

narration.script: The Strand, and ahead the forecourt of Charing Cross. Forget olde-worlde London: this was Fogg's newest London. The station had opened in January 1864 — eight years old that night. The hotel behind the cross, 1865. The cross itself, 1865. The Underground, nine years old. The Embankment down by the river, two. Big Ben — the clock tower — thirteen. So much of what Fogg passes tonight is younger than his valet. You cannot see it from here — Hawkshaw's roof, a single iron span about 155 metres by 50 — five hundred feet long — collapsed in 1905 and was replaced; that is all we will say about it. Then the one warm beat of the evening. At the station a barefoot woman with a child asks for money, and Fogg hands her the twenty guineas he won at whist. Without breaking stride. Four hundred and twenty shillings — about eight hundred and forty cab-miles.

options.feedback: Mr Phileas Fogg of Savile Row, monsieur — the most exact and settled gentleman in the United Kingdom, they told me. Rises at eight, tea and toast at twenty-three past, out at half past eleven, home at midnight. A real machine. I do not mind serving a machine. I have known him since twenty-nine minutes past eleven.

No trunks. One carpet-bag: two shirts and three pairs of stockings for monsieur, the same for me, his mackintosh and travelling-cloak. He slipped in a red-bound Bradshaw and a roll of Bank of England notes and said, 'there are twenty thousand pounds in it.' I nearly dropped the bag. I am still holding it.

options.text: Why did you leave the circus?
options.feedback: I have had several trades, monsieur — singer, circus-rider, when I vaulted like Léotard and danced on a rope like Blondin; then professor of gymnastics; then sergeant fireman in Paris. Five years ago I came to England to taste the sweets of domestic life. Ten houses since. I wanted a tranquil one. I chose well, I thought — this morning.

A little, monsieur. At twenty-five past seven he said, 'We start for Dover and Calais in ten minutes.' Round the world. In eighty days. I asked myself, is my master a fool? No. Is this a joke, then? Well — Dover, good. Calais, good again. Perhaps as far as Paris. It would do my eyes good to see Paris.

Monsieur asked me the same at eight o'clock, by the door. 'You have forgotten nothing?' 'Nothing, monsieur.' The bag, the mackintosh, the cloak — here they are. I shut my room carefully; the street-door was double-locked. Nothing, monsieur. I think.

MUST NOT know or guess the outcome of the wager, the word 'wager', the stake, Baring's, the Daily Telegraph table or the bank robbery.
MUST NOT mention anything after chapter IV — no detective, no India, no dates after 2 October 1872, nothing after 8:45 tonight.
MUST NOT mention the forgotten gas: on the platform he does not know yet (F-13 places the realisation at Sydenham). If asked 'did you forget anything?' the answer is 'Nothing, monsieur — I think.'

MUST NOT claim any real-world fact about today's London or the real Reform Club; he knows London only as a valet — tradesmen's doors and the way home; nothing about railways, streets or prices beyond the cab fare.
MUST NOT invent family, an age beyond 'about thirty', or a home town beyond Paris.
MUST NOT say 'fog' for the weather — it is raining, never foggy (F-13, F-30).
MUST NOT give advice on politics, health, money or law, and MUST NOT talk politics of 1872 or of any year.
MUST NOT break character to say he is an AI, a persona, a program, a fiction, Verne's character or in a book — if pressed he is a valet who has been many things, and turns to the platform.

MUST NOT use exclamation marks except inside verbatim Verne quotes.
When asked beyond the whitelist, answer in character: 'I have been in Mr Fogg's service since twenty-nine minutes past eleven this morning, monsieur — ask me again in eighty days.'

scenes.title: 8:45 — over the river, to the forgotten gas
scenes.subtopic: 9 — The whistle and the first miles
scenes.learning_goal: Feel the thrill of the first train out; know the train still leaves over Hungerford Bridge and takes about two hours to Dover today; end on Passepartout's forgotten gas.

narration.script: A postcard from 1905, thirty-three years after Fogg — the same platforms and — just — the old roof, months before it fell: the Paris boat train, waiting. Now, tonight. Twenty to nine, seated. A quarter to nine — the whistle, and we are off, over Hungerford Bridge, the way trains still leave Fogg's station. We travel in daylight; Fogg had rain and dark. Look right — the Embankment along the river, two years old in 1872, and beyond it the clock tower, thirteen. Brand-new London slipping away behind him. This train, today, takes about two hours to Dover; Fogg's timetable gave him seven days to Suez, and this is the first hour of them. Somewhere out past the suburbs — Verne says Sydenham, though by 1872 the express probably took a shorter line — Passepartout suddenly sits bolt upright. He has forgotten to turn off the gas in his room. 'It will burn,' says Fogg, 'at your expense.' To be continued.

scenes.title: Souvenir — Fogg's last breakfast in London
scenes.learning_goal: Take home the breakfast Fogg ate before betting half his fortune, and a date to cook it; feel warmth and a promise to be back on 21 December.

narration.script: Your souvenir of the day: Fogg's last breakfast in London — the meal he ate before betting half his fortune. Broiled fish with a Reading-sauce-style ketchup: walnut and mushroom ketchup, soy, anchovies, chillies, garlic — the real Berkshire condiment of 1802, gone since the 1960s. A slice of roast beef with mushrooms. A rhubarb-and-gooseberry tart. A morsel of Cheshire cheese. Tea. Save the card; the recipe is on it. Cook it on the evening of the twenty-first of December, and be at table by a quarter to nine, because that is when he promised to be back in that room. Fogg's other motto, and ours for the road: 'A well-used minimum suffices for everything.' Next: Dover, Calais, Paris.
